headline: York Village road redesign begins after a decade of planning and funding delays
dek: Construction is reshaping the confusing York Street-Long Sands Road triangle into a T intersection, moving a Civil War monument and changing how drivers, walkers and local businesses use the historic center.
body: Construction has started on a long-delayed redesign of York Village’s central intersection, launching a project that town officials say will make the area easier and safer to navigate while changing one of the community’s most recognizable landmarks. Crews broke ground Sept. 28, according to [Maine News Now’s report for the Portland Press Herald](https://www.pressherald.com/2026/10/08/york-village-revitalization-effort-breaks-ground-after-years-of-planning/), and are preparing to reconfigure the meeting of York Street and Long Sands Road.

The intersection is now built around a three-sided traffic triangle and narrow approaches. The project will remove that triangle and create a more conventional T intersection. Town Engineer Dean Lessard told the Press Herald that the current layout dates to an era of horse-and-buggy travel and can be confusing for people who do not regularly use the village. Town Manager Peter Joseph said officials receive complaints and hear about close calls involving people walking and driving, even though he did not describe the location as a high-accident intersection.

The work extends beyond the intersection itself. The [Town of York’s project page](https://www.yorkmaine.org/709/York-Village-Project) says construction limits run along York Street from near the Chalmers Insurance property to the York Realty Building, and along Long Sands Road from the intersection to Woodbridge Road. The town’s project page lists R.J. Grondin and Sons Construction of Gorham as the lead contractor and says the construction window is expected to run from September 2026 through November 2027. The Press Herald reports that completion is expected by late October 2027.

The finished design is intended to give pedestrians clearer routes and create a public gathering space. The existing Civil War monument will move roughly 25 to 30 feet to the east side of the intersection, where it will sit in a new pedestrian plaza. The Press Herald reports that the monument was dedicated to York by Gov. Joshua Chamberlain in 1906 and will receive a plaque explaining the move. [MaineDOT’s project description](https://www.maine.gov/dot/doing-business/bid-opportunities/02165100-york-lap-wed-03112026-1200) also includes new granite curbs, brick sidewalks, on-street parking, lighting, catch-basin and storm-drain work, landscaping and other road construction.

The transportation changes have a limit that matters for people who bike through the village. Lessard told the Press Herald that the intersection will remain narrow and will not receive dedicated bike lanes there; instead, pavement markings will identify a shared lane for cars and bicycles. MaineDOT’s broader bid summary lists bike lanes among the project elements, so the town’s description points to a distinction between the intersection itself and improvements elsewhere within the project limits. Drainage work will begin after pipes arrive, according to the newspaper.

The project’s long gestation helps explain why construction is now a major local event. Lessard said versions of a village redesign had been discussed for decades, and the current effort was revived after officials saw summer visitors struggle with the layout. York voters approved $400,000 in 2016 as the town’s 10% match for state and federal transportation money. But inflation pushed construction costs higher, leaving the town with a little more than $100,000 still to find before work could begin, Joseph told the Press Herald. The relocation of the historically significant monument also required additional review.

The redesign is already creating a separate debate about the character of the village. Residents who support clearer crossings and a more usable public space are weighing those changes against the loss of a large honey locust tree near the monument. The tree is expected to be removed by early November. Conservation Commission member James Kences objected at a joint Select Board and Planning Board meeting, while Lessard said the tree is invasive and must be removed to make the intersection safer. The disagreement shows that the project is not only an engineering exercise; it is also a decision about what York wants its historic center to look and feel like.

For nearby shops and visitors, the next year will bring construction disruption before the promised benefits arrive. The town says it will post project updates, schedule changes and construction information as the work proceeds. Officials hope the new layout, landscaping and plaza will make the village more comfortable for walking and gathering and give surrounding businesses a lift. Whether the redesign reduces confusion, improves perceived safety and supports year-round activity will become clearer only after the work is finished and people begin using the new intersection.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: York Maine village redesign begins after years of delays
seoDescription: Construction has begun on York Village’s intersection, sidewalk, drainage and public-plaza redesign, with work expected through October 2027.
